p.src: At Yojirō's urging, Sanshirō finally attended the gathering at Seiyōken. On that occasion, Sanshirō wore a black pongee haori. His mother's letter explained at length that the haori had been woven by Omitsu's mother in Miwada, then dyed with family crests and sewn by Omitsu herself. When the parcel arrived, he tried it on once, found it unappealing, and put it away in the cupboard. But Yojirō kept insisting that it would be a shame to waste it and that he simply must wear it. He seemed ready to take it away and wear it himself if Sanshirō would not, so Sanshirō ended up deciding to put it on. Once he had it on, it did not seem so bad. Dressed in this fashion, Sanshirō stood with Yojirō at the entrance to Seiyōken. According to Yojirō, this was the proper way to receive the guests. Sanshirō had not realized that was what they were doing. For one thing, he had thought of himself as a guest. Now that matters had come to this, his pongee haori made him feel like a rather shabby receptionist. He wished he had come in his uniform. Meanwhile, the members began arriving one after another. Yojirō intercepted every arrival and invariably found something to say to him. He treated every one of them like an old acquaintance. After a guest handed his hat and overcoat to an attendant and turned beside the broad staircase toward the dark corridor, Yojirō would turn to Sanshirō and tell him who the man had been. Thanks to him, Sanshirō learned the faces of quite a few eminent men. Before long, nearly all the guests had assembled. There were just under thirty of them. Professor Hirota was there too. So was Nonomiya. —Though a scientist, he was fond of painting and literature, and Haraguchi had apparently dragged him along by force on that account. Haraguchi, of course, was there as well. He had arrived before anyone else and seemed busy with everything—seeing to arrangements, dispensing charm, and now and then stroking his French-style mustache. Presently, it was time to take their seats. Each man sat wherever he pleased.

Only Yojirō and Sanshirō stayed together, taking seats near the entrance. Every other pairing of men opposite or beside one another was purely accidental.

p.src: A critic in a striped haori sat between Nonomiya and Professor Hirota. Across the table, a Doctor Shōji took his seat. He was what Yojirō called an influential professor in the humanities faculty. He was a dignified man in a frock coat. He wore his hair more than twice the usual length. Under the electric lights, it seemed to curl in black waves. It made quite a contrast with Professor Hirota's close-cropped head. Haraguchi had taken a seat some distance away. Since he was at the far corner, he faced Sanshirō directly from across the room. Around his stand-up collar, he had tied a broad strip of black satin whose flaring ends spread across his whole chest. Yojirō informed him that all French painters wore neckties like that. As Sanshirō sipped his consommé, he thought it looked exactly like the knot of a man's informal sash. Meanwhile, conversation gradually got under way. Yojirō drank beer. He was not talking as he usually did. Even a man like him appeared to be exercising a little restraint today. In a low voice Sanshirō asked, “How about a little de te fabula?” Yojirō replied, “Not today,” but immediately turned aside and began talking to the man next to him. He was thanking the man, saying something about having read that paper of his and profited greatly from it. Yet this was the very paper Yojirō had vehemently denounced in Sanshirō's presence, which struck Sanshirō as exceedingly strange. Yojirō turned back toward him. “That is quite a splendid haori. It suits you very well,” he added, making a point of examining the white crests. Just then, Haraguchi called out to Nonomiya from the far end. He was naturally loud-voiced, which made it convenient for carrying on an exchange at a distance. Professor Hirota and Professor Shōji, who until then had been conversing across the table, stopped talking for fear of interrupting their exchange.

p.src: “Nonomiya, have you finished your experiment on the pressure of light?” “No, not yet—not by a long way.” “It certainly takes a great deal of trouble. Our profession also demands patience, but yours seems even more arduous.” “Painting is easier because inspiration lets you produce a picture at once, but experiments in physics do not go so smoothly.” “I am sick to death of inspiration. This summer, as I was passing through a certain place, I heard two old women debating with each other. When I listened, I found that they were investigating whether the rainy season had ended or not. One old woman complained that in the old days the rainy season was sure to end as soon as thunder sounded, but that things no longer worked that way. Then the other grew indignant and said, ‘Good heavens, a little thunder is nowhere near enough to end it.’ —It is just the same with painting: nowadays, inspiration alone is nowhere near enough to produce a picture. Isn’t that so, Tamura? It must be the same with novels.” A novelist named Tamura was sitting beside him. The man replied that the only inspiration he ever received was a demand for overdue copy, and everyone burst out laughing. Tamura then grew serious and began asking Nonomiya whether light really exerted pressure and, if it did, how it could be tested. Nonomiya’s answer was interesting. —You make a thin disk of mica or something similar, about the size of a Sixteen Warriors playing piece, suspend it from a quartz thread, and place it in a vacuum. When the light from an arc lamp strikes the face of the disk at a right angle, the pressure of the light makes the disk move. That was how he explained it. Everyone present listened attentively. Sanshirō, in particular, thought that such a device must be inside that pickled-vegetable tin, and remembered how the telescope had astonished him when he first came to Tokyo. “Do quartz threads really exist?” he asked Yojirō in a low voice.

p.src: “Nonomiya, are there such things as quartz threads?” “Yes. You take powdered quartz— melt it in the flame of an oxyhydrogen blowpipe, then pull it apart to the left and right with both hands, and it forms a fine thread.” Sanshirō merely said, “I see,” and withdrew. This time the critic in the striped haori sitting beside Nonomiya joined the conversation. “We are utterly ignorant when it comes to such matters, but how did anyone first come upon the idea?” “It had been predicted theoretically since Maxwell, but a man named Lebedev was the first to prove it experimentally. Some people have even suggested that although a comet’s tail ought to be drawn toward the sun, the reason it always streams in the opposite direction whenever it appears may be that the pressure of light blows it away.” The critic seemed greatly impressed. “The idea is interesting, but above all, I like its grand scale,” he said. “It isn’t merely grand; it is innocent and delightful,” said Professor Hirota. “And if the idea turns out to be wrong, it will be more innocent still,” Haraguchi said with a laugh. “No, it seems the idea is probably correct. The pressure of light is proportional to the square of the radius, whereas gravitational attraction is proportional to its cube. Thus, the smaller an object becomes, the more gravity loses out and the stronger the pressure of light becomes in comparison. If a comet’s tail is composed of extremely fine particles, then it must inevitably be blown away from the sun.” Before he knew it, Nonomiya had become quite serious. Then Haraguchi said in his usual manner, “It may be innocent, but the calculations have become terribly troublesome. There is a drawback to every advantage after all.” At this remark, everyone returned to their former beer-drinking mood. Professor Hirota said the following.

p.src: “It seems a physicist cannot afford to be a naturalist.” The words “physicist” and “naturalist” aroused considerable interest throughout the gathering.

u.src: “It seems a physicist cannot afford to be a naturalist.” The words “physicist” and “naturalist” aroused considerable interest throughout the gathering.

p.src: “What do you mean by that?” Nonomiya himself asked. Professor Hirota found himself obliged to explain. “Well, if you want to test the pressure of light, it’s no use merely opening your eyes and observing nature. The fact of light pressure does not seem to be printed anywhere on nature’s menu, does it? So you artificially arrange apparatus involving quartz threads, a vacuum, mica, and the like, contriving matters so that the pressure becomes visible to the physicist’s eye. That means you’re no naturalist.” “But hardly a romantic either,” Haraguchi interjected teasingly. “No, he is a romantic,” Professor Hirota declared with solemn self-importance. “What could be more romantic than placing light and the object receiving it in a spatial relationship never found in the ordinary natural world?” “But once they have been placed in that relationship, all he does is observe the pressure inherent in the light, so from that point on he is a naturalist, surely,” Nonomiya said. “Then a physicist is a romantic naturalist. In literature, wouldn’t that make him something like Ibsen?” said the doctor across the way, offering a comparison. “Indeed. Ibsen’s plays employ apparatus as elaborate as Nonomiya’s, but whether the characters operating within that apparatus obey natural laws as light does is open to doubt.” This observation came from the critic in the striped haori. “That may be so, but I think there is one thing we ought to remember when studying human beings. Namely, that a human being placed in a given situation possesses both the capacity and the power to act in the opposite direction. That is what I mean. Yet we have the peculiar habit of assuming that human beings and rays of light alike act in obedience to mechanical laws, and this sometimes leads to extraordinary errors.

p.src: “Then it follows that whatever a given person may do under given circumstances is natural,” the novelist across the way said, putting it as a question. Professor Hirota answered at once, “Yes, yes. However you portray whatever sort of person, isn’t there likely to be at least one such individual somewhere in the world?” “After all, being human ourselves, we cannot possibly imagine actions or conduct that are altogether inhuman. Isn’t it merely poor writing that makes a character seem less than human?” At that, the novelist fell silent. Now the doctor spoke again. “Even among physicists, when Galileo notices that the time taken by one swing of a hanging lamp in a church remains the same regardless of the size of the oscillation, or Newton discovers that an apple falls through gravity, they are naturalists from the very beginning.” “That sort of naturalism would be perfectly welcome in literature too. Haraguchi, is there a naturalist school in painting as well?” Nonomiya asked. “Of course there is. There’s a formidable fellow called Courbet. Vérité vraie. Nothing short of fact will satisfy him. But his kind has not become overwhelmingly rampant. It is merely acknowledged as one school among others. And it would be troublesome if that were not so. The same must be true of fiction, wouldn’t you say? Surely there must also be writers resembling Moreau and Puvis de Chavannes.” “There must indeed,” replied the novelist beside him. After dinner there were no speeches at the table or anything of the sort. Haraguchi merely kept denouncing the statue up at Kudan. If statues like that were erected indiscriminately, he said, the citizens of Tokyo would suffer for it. His view was that it would show far better taste to make a statue of a beautiful geisha instead. Yojirō told Sanshirō that the statue at Kudan had been made by a man who was on bad terms with Haraguchi.

Sanshirō replied that he probably had. The two of them watched the moon from the top of Suribachiyama and then went home.

p.src: On the way back, Yojirō suddenly began making excuses to Sanshirō about the money he owed him. It was a relatively cold night under a brilliantly clear moon. Sanshirō had scarcely been thinking about the money at all. He was not even listening seriously to the excuses. He assumed it would never be repaid anyway. Nor did Yojirō ever say that he would repay it. He merely offered one explanation after another for why he could not. Sanshirō found his manner of telling it all far more entertaining. —A certain man he knew had suffered a broken heart, grown sick of the world, and finally resolved to kill himself; but he disliked the sea, disliked rivers, disliked volcanic craters even more, and hated the idea of hanging most of all, so he had no choice but to buy a pistol. After buying it, but before he had carried out his purpose, a friend came to borrow money. He refused, saying he had no money, but the friend pleaded with him to find some way to help, so he reluctantly lent him his precious pistol. The friend pawned it and thereby weathered his immediate difficulties. By the time the friend had raised the money, redeemed the pistol, and brought it back, its owner no longer wished to die. Thus it amounted to saying that the man's life had been saved because someone came to borrow money from him. “You see, such things do happen,” said Yojirō. To Sanshirō, it was merely funny. It meant nothing else to him. He looked up at the moon high overhead and laughed aloud. Even without getting his money back, he felt cheerful. “You mustn't laugh,” Yojirō admonished him. This made Sanshirō laugh all the more. “Stop laughing and think about it carefully. It was precisely because I didn't repay you that you were able to borrow money from Mineko, wasn't it?” Sanshirō stopped laughing. “And?” “Isn't that more than enough? —You're in love with her, aren't you?” Yojirō knew him well.

p.src: “Have you paid her back yet?” “No.” “Keep borrowing it from her forever.” He spoke with complete nonchalance. Sanshirō made no reply. But of course he had no intention of keeping the money indefinitely. In fact, after paying the necessary twenty yen to his lodging house, he had meant to take the remaining ten yen to the Satomis' the very next day; but then he reconsidered, deciding that repaying it at once would actually go against her kindness and would be ungracious, and so he had turned back even at the cost of giving up a precious opportunity to enter their gate. Then, somehow or other, his resolve had weakened and he had broken into the ten yen. Indeed, that evening's meeting fee had come out of it. And not only his own. Yojirō's had come out of it as well. Only two or three yen now remained. Sanshirō meant to use it to buy a winter undershirt. The truth was that, since Yojirō seemed altogether unlikely to repay him, Sanshirō had recently taken the plunge and asked his family back home to make up a shortfall of thirty yen. Since he received ample money for his studies every month, he could hardly ask for more merely by saying that he was short. Sanshirō was not a man accustomed to lying, so he was at a loss when it came to giving a reason for the request. With no other choice, he simply wrote that a friend had lost his money and was in distress, and that, feeling sorry for him, he had lent him some. As a result, he himself was now in distress. He asked them please to send him the money. If they had replied at once, it ought to have arrived by now, yet it still had not come. Thinking that it might perhaps have arrived that very evening, he returned to his lodging and found, just as he had hoped, an envelope addressed in his mother's hand lying squarely on his desk. Strangely, although such letters always came by registered mail, today this one bore only a single three-sen stamp. When he opened it, he found the letter unusually brief.

With no other choice, he simply wrote that a friend had lost his money and was in distress, and that, feeling sorry for him, he had lent him some.
As a result, he himself was now in distress.
He asked them please to send him the money.
If they had replied at once, it ought to have arrived by now, yet it still had not come.
Thinking that it might perhaps have arrived that very evening, he returned to his lodging and found, just as he had hoped, an envelope addressed in his mother's hand lying squarely on his desk.

p.src: Sanshirō did not visit Nonomiya the next day or the day after. Nor did Nonomiya send him any word. In this way, about a week passed. At last Nonomiya sent a letter by the maid from Sanshirō's lodging house. It said that he had something entrusted to him by Sanshirō's mother and asked Sanshirō to come over for a moment. Finding an interval between lectures, Sanshirō descended once more into the College of Science basement. He had hoped to settle the matter in a brief conversation while standing there, but things did not go so smoothly. In the room that Nonomiya had occupied all by himself that summer, there were now two or three bearded men. There were also two or three students in uniform. All of them were absorbed in their research, working in silence and utterly indifferent to the sunlit world above their heads. Of them all, Nonomiya appeared the busiest. He glanced at Sanshirō, who had shown his face at the doorway, and approached him without a word. “Some money has arrived from home, so come and collect it. I don't have it with me here. And there are some other things I want to discuss with you.” Sanshirō answered, “All right.” He asked whether that evening would do. Nonomiya thought for a moment, then finally made up his mind and said that would be fine. With that, Sanshirō left the basement. On his way out, he marveled that scientists were indeed remarkably patient people. The jar of fukujinzuke pickles and the telescope that he had seen that summer were still installed in precisely their former positions. When Sanshirō met Yojirō at the next lecture and told him what had happened, Yojirō looked at him as if only just refraining from calling him a fool. “That's why I told you to keep the money as long as you could. You meddle needlessly and make the old folks worry. And then Sōhachi lectures you. Nothing could be more foolish.” He spoke as though he did not acknowledge in the least that the whole affair had begun with him.

p.src: “I didn't want to keep borrowing it indefinitely, so I wrote home and said so.” “You may not like it, but they would be pleased.” “Why?” To Sanshirō himself, that “why” sounded somewhat false. But it seemed to have no effect whatever on the other man. “Isn't it obvious? It would be the same if I were in their place. Suppose I had money to spare. In that case, I would feel better leaving the money on loan to you than having you pay it back. You see, people like to be as kind as they can to others, so long as it causes them no hardship.” Sanshirō made no reply and began taking notes on the lecture. After he had written two or three lines, Yojirō again brought his mouth close to Sanshirō's ear. “Even I have often lent money to people when I had some. But not one of them has ever paid me back. That is why I am as cheerful as you see me now.” Sanshirō could hardly say, “I see.” He merely gave a faint smile and set his pen moving again. After that, Yojirō too settled down and said nothing until the class ended. When the bell rang and the two of them left the classroom side by side, Yojirō suddenly asked a question. “Is that woman in love with you?” A steady stream of students was filing out behind them. Sanshirō had no choice but to remain silent as he descended the steep stairs, passed through the side entrance, and emerged onto the open ground beside the library; only then did he turn to Yojirō. “I'm not really sure.” Yojirō looked at Sanshirō for a while. “That can happen. But even if you knew for certain, could you become that woman's husband?” Sanshirō had never once considered this question. He had felt that the mere fact of being loved by Mineko was his sole qualification for becoming her husband. Now that Yojirō had put it that way, it did indeed seem open to question.

p.src: “Nonomiya could become one,” Yojirō said. “Has there ever been anything between Nonomiya and her?” Sanshirō’s face was as solemn as though it had been carved that way. “Don’t know,” Yojirō replied curtly. Sanshirō remained silent. “Go back to Nonomiya and listen to another of his sermons,” Yojirō tossed over his shoulder as he started toward the pond. Sanshirō stood rooted to the spot like a signboard advertising stupidity. Yojirō went five or six paces, then came back laughing. “Why don’t you just marry Yoshiko?” he said, taking Sanshirō by the arm and leading him toward the pond. As they walked, he repeated twice, “She’d make a fine wife, a fine wife.” Before long, the bell rang again. That evening Sanshirō set out for Nonomiya’s house, but as it was still a little too early, he strolled as far as Fourth Street and entered a large foreign-goods shop to buy a shirt. A shopboy brought out various shirts from the back, but Sanshirō merely felt them and unfolded them, showing no readiness to buy. While he lingered there with an air of unaccountable leisure, Mineko and Yoshiko happened to come in together to buy perfume. After greeting him with an exclamation of surprise, Mineko said, “Thank you for the other day.” Sanshirō understood perfectly what she was thanking him for. The day after borrowing money from Mineko, he ought to have called on her again and returned the surplus at once; instead, he had postponed doing so, waited two days, and sent her a carefully worded letter of thanks. The wording of the letter did honestly express its writer’s feelings at the time, but he had of course said too much. Sanshirō piled up every phrase he could muster to express his gratitude with passionate intensity. It was so fervent that an ordinary reader would scarcely have taken it for a letter thanking someone for a loan.

p.src: Yet it contained nothing but gratitude. For that very reason, gratitude had naturally swelled into something more than gratitude. When Sanshirō dropped the letter into the postbox, he expected an immediate reply from Mineko. But the painstakingly prepared letter had simply gone off and vanished without a response. p.src: The two women came over laughing and helped him look at the shirts. At last Yoshiko said, “Choose this one.” Sanshirō took that one. This time it was Sanshirō who was asked for advice about perfume. He knew nothing about it. He picked up a bottle labeled “Heliotrope” and casually asked, “How about this one?” Mineko immediately decided, “Let’s take it.” Sanshirō almost felt sorry for her. When they went outside and were about to part, the women began bowing to each other. When Yoshiko said, “Well, off you go,” Mineko replied, “Don’t be long…” Listening to them, Sanshirō learned that the younger sister was on her way to her brother’s lodgings. Thus Sanshirō found himself facing another evening walk toward Oiwake in the company of a beautiful woman. The sun had not yet completely set. It was not walking with Yoshiko that troubled Sanshirō so much as having to arrive with her at Nonomiya’s lodgings. He wondered whether he might simply go home tonight and come back another time. Still, if he was to hear what Yojirō called a sermon, it might be useful to have Yoshiko beside him. Surely Nonomiya would not openly admonish him before someone else, saying that his mother had made such a request. Perhaps he might get away with merely accepting the money. —Sanshirō made this slightly underhanded resolution to himself. “I’m on my way to Mr. Nonomiya’s too.” “Oh, for a social visit?” “No, I have a little business to attend to. Are you going for pleasure?” “No, I have business too.” They had asked virtually the same question and received virtually the same answer. Yet neither showed the slightest sign of being inconvenienced. To make sure, Sanshirō asked whether he would be intruding. She said he would not be intruding in the least.

p.src: “Did you buy the violin?” “How did you know?” Sanshirō was at a loss for an answer. Paying no attention to his difficulty, the woman immediately continued: “No matter how often I asked my brother, all he ever said was that he would buy me one, but he never did.” Inwardly, Sanshirō blamed Yojirō rather than Nonomiya or Hirota. The two turned off the Oiwake road into a narrow lane. Inside the lane stood a great many houses. Eave lamps at each doorway lit the dark road. They stopped before one of those lamps. Nonomiya lived farther inside. It was only about one chō from Sanshirō’s lodgings. Since Nonomiya had moved here, Sanshirō had visited him two or three times. Nonomiya’s quarters consisted of two secluded rooms on the left, reached by going to the end of a broad corridor and climbing two steps straight ahead. Facing south, with someone else’s large garden extending almost beneath the veranda, it was exceedingly quiet both day and night. It was such a comfortable place that, from the first time he saw Mr. Nonomiya ensconced in these detached rooms, Sanshirō had been impressed by the thought that giving up one’s own household and taking lodgings was not such a bad idea after all. On that occasion Mr. Nonomiya had stepped down into the corridor, looked up from below at the eaves of his room, and said, “Just look—it’s thatched.” Sure enough, unusually, there were no tiles on the roof. Tonight, of course, the roof was invisible in the darkness, but an electric light was burning inside the room. The instant Sanshirō saw the electric light, he remembered the thatched roof. It struck him as amusing. “What an odd pair of visitors to turn up together. Did you meet at the entrance?” Mr. Nonomiya asked his sister. His sister explained that they had not. While she was at it, she advised him to buy a shirt like Sanshirō’s. Then she said that the violin from the other day was Japanese-made and its tone was too poor to be any good.

p.src: “Your mother was worried and sent me a long letter. She says that Sanshirō claims he was obliged by unavoidable circumstances to lend his monthly school allowance to a friend, but that even a friend should not borrow money so recklessly, and if he did borrow it, he ought surely to repay it. Country people are honest, so one can hardly blame her for thinking that way. And then, she says, even if Sanshirō was going to lend money, he went much too far about it. She writes that for someone whose parents send him his school expenses every month to advance twenty or thirty yen at a time to others is utterly imprudent—but the way she writes it makes it sound as though I were somehow responsible, which puts me in an awkward position. …” Nonomiya looked at Sanshirō with a broad, knowing grin. Sanshirō merely replied in all seriousness, “I am sorry to have put you in such a position.” Apparently Nonomiya had not meant to rebuke the young man outright, for he softened his tone a little. “Oh, there is nothing to worry about. It is nothing of any consequence. It is only that your mother values money according to country standards, so thirty yen assumes tremendous weight for her. She wrote that thirty yen would somehow feed a family of four for half a year. Is that really so, my boy?” he asked. Yoshiko burst into loud laughter. Sanshirō too found the absurdity of it extremely amusing; but his mother’s assertion was not a tale wholly divorced from fact, and when he realized this, he regretted somewhat that he had acted so rashly. “That would make five yen a month, or one yen and twenty-five sen per person. Divided over thirty days, that comes to about four sen a day—surely that is a little too cheap, even for the country,” Nonomiya calculated.

p.src: “What would they have to eat to live on so little?” Yoshiko asked earnestly. With no time left to regret what he had said, Sanshirō told her all sorts of things about country life as he knew it. Among them was a custom called miyagomori, keeping vigil at the village shrine. At that time, one person from each of the sixty households would turn out; all sixty would take the day off, gather at the village shrine, drink without stopping from morning till night, and feast continuously on delicacies.

At that time, one person from each of the sixty households would turn out; all sixty would take the day off, gather at the village shrine, drink without stopping from morning till night, and feast continuously on delicacies.

p.src: “And all that for ten yen?” Yoshiko exclaimed in astonishment. The sermon seemed to have vanished somewhere in the course of this. They chatted idly for a while, and when the conversation reached a pause, Nonomiya began again in a more formal tone. “Anyway, as far as Mother is concerned— she wanted me first to look into the circumstances and, if I found nothing amiss, to give you the money. And she wants me, troublesome though it may be, to let her know the particulars. But I handed the money over before asking anything at all—so what are we to do? You did lend it to Sasaki, didn’t you?” Sanshirō concluded that Mineko had let it slip to Yoshiko, who in turn had told Nonomiya. Yet neither brother nor sister realized that, after passing from hand to hand, the money had transformed itself into a violin, and this gave Sanshirō a curious feeling. He merely answered, “Yes.” “I hear Sasaki bought betting tickets and lost all his own money.” “Yes.” Yoshiko burst into loud laughter again. “Well then, I’ll give Mother some suitable account of it. But from now on, you had better stop lending money like that.” Sanshirō replied that he would do so, exchanged farewells, and was just beginning to rise when Yoshiko announced that she, too, was going home. “You have to tell me about what we discussed earlier,” her brother reminded her. “There’s no need,” his sister refused. “Yes, there is.” “No, there isn’t. I don’t know.” Her brother looked at her face and fell silent. His sister spoke again. “But there’s nothing I can do about it, is there? What is the use of asking whether I’ll go to someone I don’t even know? I neither like him nor dislike him, so there’s simply nothing I can say. That’s why I don’t know.” At last Sanshirō understood what she truly meant by “I don’t know.” Leaving the brother and sister as they were, he hurried outside.

p.src: He passed through the deserted alley, lit only by the lamps beneath the eaves, and emerged onto the main street, where the wind was blowing. When he turned to face north, it struck him full in the face. At intervals it blew from the direction of his lodgings. At that moment Sanshirō had a thought. Nonomiya would probably escort his sister through this wind all the way to Satomi. He climbed to the second floor of his lodgings, entered his room, and sat down; the sound of the wind was still there. Whenever Sanshirō heard wind like this, the word “fate” came to mind. Each time it came roaring, he felt like shrinking back. He had never thought himself a strong man. When he considered it, nearly everything that had shaped his fate since coming to Tokyo had been Yojirō’s doing. And it had been shaped so that, to some degree, he was always being amiably tossed about. Yojirō was a lovable mischief-maker. Sanshirō felt that this lovable mischief-maker would probably continue to hold his fate in his hands. The wind blew incessantly. It was certainly a wind more powerful than Yojirō. Sanshirō placed the thirty yen his mother had sent beside his pillow and went to bed. These thirty yen, too, had been born of fate’s caprice. He had no idea at all what part the money would play from now on. He was going to return it to Mineko. When Mineko accepted it, another gust was certain to come. Sanshirō hoped it would be as great a gust as possible. With that, Sanshirō fell asleep. He sank into a sleep so sound that neither fate nor Yojirō could meddle with it. Then the clang of the fire bell woke him. Voices could be heard somewhere. This was the second fire he had witnessed in Tokyo. Sanshirō threw a haori over his nightclothes and opened the window. The wind had subsided considerably. Amid the moaning of the wind, the two-story house opposite looked pitch-black. The blacker the house appeared, the redder the sky behind it glowed.

p.src: Sanshirō endured the cold and gazed at that red glow for a while. At that moment, fate appeared vividly red in Sanshirō's mind. Sanshirō burrowed back beneath the warm quilt. And he forgot the fates of all the people whirling madly within that crimson destiny.

p.src: When morning came, he was his usual self again. He put on his uniform, took his notebook, and set off for school. But he did not forget to put the thirty yen in his pocket. Unfortunately, his class schedule was inconvenient. It was packed solid until three. If he went after three, Yoshiko would probably already be home from school. Her brother, Kyōsuke Satomi, might possibly be at home as well. He felt that if anyone else was there, he would be utterly unable to return the money. Yojirō spoke to him again. “Did you hear the sermon last night?” “It was hardly what you would call a sermon.” “I thought not. Nonomiya is a reasonable man, for all that,” he said, and went off somewhere. They met again two hours later, during a lecture. “Things with Professor Hirota look certain to work out well,” Yojirō said. When Sanshirō asked how far matters had progressed, Yojirō replied, “Oh, there is no need to worry. I will tell you all about it when we have time. The professor was asking about you, saying you had not visited for some time. You ought to go and see him now and then. The professor lives alone, you know. We must keep him company. Bring him something next time.” With that parting instruction, he vanished again. Then, during the next period, he appeared again from somewhere. For some reason, in the middle of the lecture, he suddenly scribbled on a blank sheet of paper, as tersely as a telegram, “Did you get the money?” and passed it over. Sanshirō was about to write a reply, but when he looked toward the instructor, he found the man staring directly at him. He crumpled the paper into a ball and tossed it beneath his feet. Only after waiting for the lecture to end did he finally reply. “I got the money. I have it here.” “You did? Good. “Are you going to return it?” “Of course I am.” “That would be best.
